newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Russian liberal warns wider NATO could harm reform.
newsitem.headline: Russian liberal warns wider NATO could harm reform.

text.p: A leading Russian liberal warned on Saturday that if NATO were to admit former Soviet bloc countries, a move fiercely opposed by Moscow, it could harm the cause of reform in the country.

The warning, from Alexander Shokhin who is first deputy chairman of the Russian parliament and a former deputy prime minister for the economy, was the latest in a barrage at the World Economic Forum against NATO's expansion plans.
"We would like other countries to take Russia's views into account when major global decisions are being taken," he told a session devoted to his country's place in the world.

"If NATO extends its frontiers to our borders without due consideration of Russia's position, I fear public opinion would make it difficult for the reformers to continue reforms at the present pace," he said.

The caution from Shokhin, seen as one of the most Western- oriented officials around ailing President Boris Yeltsin, followed more trenchant comments on the expansion issue in Davos by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and the deputy foreign minister, Alexander Avdeyev.

Chernomyrdin, who has had talks on the fringes of the annual gathering of global business and political leaders with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, said the plan would create a new dividing line across Europe.

He added that Solana, who has argued there was no threat to Russia implicit in the move, "is wrong". He contented that the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation had not changed its basic nature since Cold War days.

Shokhin did not expand on his remarks, but it clearly reflected concern among leading liberal reformers that NATO expansion, especially if it took in former Soviet states, could give new life to communist and nationalist sentiment in Russia.

Avdeyev said on Friday the alliance, which is due to take in Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary later this year, could not move Moscow to accept enlargement by vowing not to put troops or nuclear weapons on new members' soil.
He accused the NATO of clinging to decades-old military doctrine that saw Moscow as its most dangerous potential enemy.

Russia argues that it should be admitted to full membership of the alliance, bringing current membership from 16 to 17. But this is strongly opposed by the United States -- and some countries of the old Soviet empire.

Speaking before Avdeyev, Solana reiterated NATO's plan to embrace former Soviet-led Warsaw Pact countries at a Madrid summit in July. After the three leading candidates, Romania, Slovenia and Bulgaria are hoping for admission.

The Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia -- all former Soviet republics and for Moscow even more politically sensitive than its old East European Cold War allies -- have also made it known they would like to join.
Solana stressed NATO sought to build good ties with Moscow that acknowledged Russia's importance for European security.

But Avdeyev said that, although efforts to build closer ties were going well on the political and diplomatic level, they broke down when it came to military doctrine, which he alleged NATO had not changed essentially since the 1970s.
"If NATO takes on new members on the basis of military thinking from the 1970s, it gives us in Russia the impression that we are being asked to jump backward in time to 20 years ago," he said.
